title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content, including deepfake images and video, was used to fabricate a news interview that never took place. The failure is not in a deployed AI product built by a legitimate company but in the offensive use of generative AI tools by scammers to produce convincing false media at scale. The system involved sits entirely outside licensed financial services infrastructure, which is precisely what makes it hard to intercept before victims act on it.

The point of failure is upstream of any platform check: fake articles, fake websites, and fake advertisements are assembled into a coordinated web before regulators or hosting platforms typically see them. Catching this earlier would have required either automated detection of synthetic media by the platforms distributing the content, or faster takedown pipelines, neither of which prevented the 19,400 scams ASIC removed in the reported period. The 182 percent increase in removals indicates the volume is growing faster than current countermeasures contain it.

What is not established is the identity of those responsible, the total financial harm caused to consumers, or whether any individual was successfully prosecuted. ASIC's warnings and removal figures are regulatory reports, not findings of liability against named parties.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article claimed that Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article never actually occurred, representing a growing trend of AI-generated investment scams. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research reveals these schemes are becoming more sophisticated and prevalent, using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to deceive consumers.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Alan Kohler is among the most impersonated Australians, alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, and billionaire Gina Rinehart. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake websites, news articles, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that familiar branding and testimonials do not guarantee legitimacy.
